r: HSL 1030 trains students to design, implement, and evaluate sport and motor programs for people with physical, mental, or multiple disabilities and for aging populations, mapping to O*NET's Training and Teaching Others and Assisting and Caring for Others activities. The instrumental work is embodied: reading a participant's real-time physical response, adapting cueing, spotting, and modifying equipment mid-session for an individual with a disability. Task-exposure research explicitly classifies manual and physical work as low-exposure, and the interpersonal, real-time nature of adaptive instruction sits outside any current model's competent range. The binding constraint is direct physical presence with a vulnerable population, where verification burden is high because a misjudged cue or unsupervised transition carries real injury risk. At this horizon AI plausibly assists only the peripheral paperwork — session logs, generic activity templates — not the instrumental skill the course teaches.

By 2031 AI systems will likely produce stronger draft program plans, progress-tracking summaries, and individualized activity suggestions for special-population fitness, narrowing the administrative half of this course's workload; the Anthropic Economic Index already shows writing and documentation tasks concentrated in current usage, and that pattern plausibly extends into program-planning paperwork. But the instrumental task — physically teaching a person with a disability a motor skill, adjusting spotting technique in real time, reading nonverbal distress signals — remains outside deployable AI competence, and task-exposure research continues to treat manual, physically supervised work as low-exposure. Verification burden stays high: an AI-suggested activity modification for someone with a physical impairment still needs a qualified human to confirm safety before use. Adoption of AI tools in adaptive recreation settings specifically also likely lags general diffusion figures, given the specialized, small-scale nature of these programs.

A ten-year horizon is genuinely uncertain: METR/Epoch capability trends imply AI systems handling far longer, more autonomous task sequences than today, and it is plausible that adaptive-program design and outcome documentation become largely AI-drafted with light human review. Even so, the physically embodied core of this course — hands-on demonstration, spotting, and moment-to-moment adjustment for a person with a disability during activity — is not the kind of task current capability trajectories suggest closing by 2036; no described technology performs psychomotor instruction or in-person behavioral judgment for this population. Firm-level diffusion data already shows adoption trailing far behind raw capability, and specialized adaptive-recreation settings, serving small, high-vulnerability populations, are unlikely to be early adopters even if general-purpose tools advance substantially. The safety-critical verification burden of working with disabled and aging participants keeps a human instructor structurally necessary regardless of how capable underlying models become.
HSL 1030.d: This course is intended for HPS majors and minors. The emphasis of this course is on sport and motor programs for special populations and programs related to those individuals with physical, mental, or multiple disabilities as well as the aging population. This course will include opportunities for experience in designing, implementing, and evaluating existing sports and physical activity programs for the disabled.

r: HSL 1250 prepares students to teach adapted aquatic instruction to people with mental and physical disabilities and leads directly to Red Cross Adaptive Aquatic certification, building on Water Safety Instructor credentials students already hold. The instrumental task is in-water, real-time safety supervision and stroke instruction adapted to individual disabilities — reading fatigue, panic, or seizure risk and intervening physically within seconds. This maps to O*NET's Training and Teaching Others and Monitoring Processes, Materials, or Surroundings activities, both life-safety functions no current AI system performs. Task-exposure research explicitly treats manual, physically supervised work as low-exposure, and here the binding constraint is doubly strong: a named certification body gates the credential, and verification burden is maximal because an error in water with a disabled swimmer is immediately dangerous, not merely costly to correct. Nothing in current deployment data suggests this instructional function is even a candidate for automation at this horizon.

By 2031, drafting written lesson plans or logging swimmer progress for the certification pathway may see modest AI assistance, echoing how the Anthropic Economic Index shows writing and documentation tasks already concentrated in current usage. That does not touch the instrumental core: in-pool instruction of disabled swimmers still requires a certified human physically present to demonstrate adapted strokes, provide hands-on support, and make split-second safety judgments no remote or embodied AI system can credibly perform at scale. The binding constraint tightens rather than loosens — the Red Cross certification structure names required practical, in-water competencies that a governing body must sign off on, functioning like other institutional brakes such as clinical-hour mandates elsewhere in health-adjacent fields. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge reliability outside a model's competence is especially dangerous here, where miscalibrated trust in an AI safety recommendation could put a vulnerable swimmer at risk.

Ten years out, general model capability will almost certainly be far greater by METR/Epoch trend extrapolations, but capability growth does not by itself relocate a certifying body's practical in-water requirements, and nothing currently visible suggests the Red Cross Adaptive Aquatic credential will drop its hands-on demonstration component. The instructional task this course teaches — physically present, real-time safety supervision of disabled swimmers — remains embodied and psychomotor in a way no described AI trajectory reaches; task-exposure research's core distinction between manual/physical and cognitive work is not expected to dissolve merely because underlying models get more capable. Diffusion data already shows AI adoption lagging capability broadly, and adoption in small, safety-regulated instructional niches like adaptive aquatics plausibly lags further still. The strongest hedge is that documentation and certification administration could be substantially reshaped, but the core instrumental reason a student takes this course — becoming a competent in-water adaptive instructor — appears durable.
HSL 1250.d: This course acquaints the student with various adapted aquatic programs and methods of teaching the mentally and/or physically disabled. The course leads to Red Cross Adaptive Aquatic certification.

r: HSL 1340 develops skill in designing, implementing, and evaluating rhythmic and adapted-dance activities for people who are auditorially or visually impaired, emotionally disturbed, physically or mentally handicapped, or aged, applied within recreation and rehabilitation settings. The instrumental work maps to O*NET's Training and Teaching Others and Assisting and Caring for Others activities and consists of embodied movement instruction — physically demonstrating adapted rhythm patterns, modifying cues for sensory or cognitive impairment, and reading a participant's real-time emotional and physical response during a session. Task-exposure research classifies manual and physically interactive work as low-exposure, and that classification fits this course closely: no deployed model performs movement-based rehabilitative instruction with a live, vulnerable participant. Verification burden is elevated because a poorly adapted cue for someone with a sensory or emotional impairment can cause real harm, reinforcing that direct human presence, not documentation, is the binding constraint here.

By 2031, AI tools may help generate adapted-activity ideas or draft session outlines faster, consistent with productivity research showing large speed gains on drafting-style tasks, but selecting and physically delivering a rhythm activity to a person with a specific sensory or emotional impairment still depends on in-the-room judgment about that individual's tolerance and response. Task-exposure research's finding that physically interactive work stays low-exposure should hold at this horizon, since rehabilitative movement instruction requires continuous embodied feedback a text or even multimodal system cannot obtain from a live body in a room. Verification burden remains a real constraint: an AI-suggested modification for someone who is visually impaired or emotionally disturbed still needs a trained instructor to judge appropriateness before use, and the jagged-frontier evidence on miscalibrated trust argues against leaning on unverified AI suggestions in a therapeutic movement context. Broader AI diffusion into small-scale adaptive recreation programs likely remains partial.

A decade out under METR/Epoch capability-growth extrapolations, AI could plausibly generate highly individualized adapted-activity curricula and track participant progress with considerable sophistication, further compressing the planning side of adapted-dance and rhythm instruction. But the delivery task this course centers on — physically leading a rhythm or movement activity with someone who has a sensory, cognitive, or emotional impairment, adjusting in real time to their embodied response — sits squarely in the category task-exposure research treats as durably low-exposure, and no visible capability trend targets psychomotor, in-person rehabilitative instruction specifically. Firm-level diffusion evidence already shows adoption trailing capability by a wide margin, and specialized recreation-therapy contexts serving small, vulnerable populations are plausible late adopters even under optimistic capability assumptions. The honest position is substantial uncertainty about administrative and planning support, paired with high confidence that the embodied instructional core remains a human function.
HSL 1340.d: This course emphasizes skills for the development, implementation, and evaluation of rhythmic activities for the handicapped in recreation and rehabilitation programs. The course will also cover a variety of adapted dance, and movement techniques for the auditorially and visually impaired, emotionally disturbed, physically handicapped, mentally handicapped, and the aged.

r: HSL 1420 builds skill in developing, implementing, and evaluating fitness and activity programs for older adults, with field observation and hands-on involvement at recreation agencies or health care facilities in the Denver area. The instrumental tasks split across O*NET's Training and Teaching Others, Assisting and Caring for Others, and Organizing, Planning, and Prioritizing Work — the last of these (drafting a program outline, sequencing activities) is more cognitively tractable than the in-person supervision and instruction components. Observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical and writing-adjacent tasks dominate current AI use, suggesting near-term assistance concentrates on program-planning documentation rather than direct elder instruction. The binding constraint remains the field-placement structure: this course requires physical presence at an agency or facility working with older adults, where fall risk, cognitive status, and mobility limitations demand real-time human judgment. Verification burden is meaningful given the elevated injury risk in exercise programming for frail older adults.

By 2031, program-design and evaluation paperwork for elder fitness programming plausibly becomes substantially AI-assisted, in line with professional-writing productivity research showing large time savings alongside quality gains on drafting tasks; a student might reasonably draft an activity plan with AI support and spend more time on delivery. That delivery — leading exercise activities with older adults who may have balance, cardiac, or cognitive limitations, observed in real agency and facility settings — is not close to automatable; task-exposure research continues to treat hands-on, physically supervised work as low-exposure regardless of gains in adjacent planning tasks. Field placement itself functions as an institutional brake, since the course's structure requires physical presence at an outside facility, similar in kind (though not degree) to clinical-hour requirements found elsewhere in health-adjacent programs. Verification burden stays elevated: exercise modifications for frail older adults carry real fall and cardiac risk that a human supervisor must confirm.

A ten-year projection has to hold two things at once: METR/Epoch trend lines suggest AI systems handling much longer planning and evaluation workflows for elder-fitness programming with limited human input, while the delivery side of this course — hands-on activity leadership with older adults in real facilities, judging fatigue, balance, and cognitive engagement moment to moment — plausibly stays outside deployable AI competence given its embodied, real-time character. Task-exposure research's association of manual and physically supervised work with lower exposure gives no reason to expect that gap to close purely from general capability gains. Diffusion data already shows AI adoption well behind raw capability at the firm level, and small community and health care facilities serving older adults are unlikely early adopters of embodied AI tools even a decade out. The most defensible position is that this course's field-placement and hands-on-delivery components remain the instrumental reason to take it, even as planning work is increasingly AI-assisted.
HSL 1420.d: This course emphasizes skills for the development, implementation and evaluation of activities and fitness programs for older persons in various settings. This course will include opportunities for observation and involvement with various recreation agencies or health care facilities in the Denver area.

r: HSL 1430 covers methods and techniques for running camps serving special populations and for outdoor recreational outings, an embodied leadership role mapping to O*NET's Training and Teaching Others, Performing General Physical Activities, and Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others. The instrumental task is in-the-field camp leadership — supervising outdoor activities, adapting techniques to participants' physical or cognitive needs, and managing group safety in an outdoor, often remote setting. Task-exposure research is explicit that manual, physically situated work is low-exposure, and outdoor camp leadership with a special-needs population sits firmly in that category; no deployed AI system can supervise or physically adapt an outdoor activity in real time. Verification burden is elevated because outdoor settings compound the risk already present when working with people who have disabilities, and remoteness from immediate backup support raises the cost of any misjudgment. The course description is brief, so confidence in fine-grained task detail is limited.

By 2031, AI may help with camp logistics documentation — packing lists, activity schedules, risk-assessment templates — a plausible extension of the drafting-task speedups seen in productivity research on professional writing. That leaves untouched the instrumental skill this course targets: leading outdoor activities and camp routines for people with disabilities in real time, in physical environments with limited infrastructure and no immediate technical support. Task-exposure research's treatment of physical, hands-on work as low-exposure should still apply, since outdoor camp supervision cannot be performed remotely or virtually and depends on continuous embodied judgment about participants and terrain. Verification burden remains high given the compounded risk of outdoor settings plus special-needs supervision, and the jagged-frontier finding on miscalibrated trust argues against relying on AI-generated risk assessments without expert review in this setting. Given the course description's brevity, this projection carries somewhat more uncertainty than for courses with more detailed task descriptions.

Looking to 2036, capability-trend extrapolations from METR/Epoch imply substantially more autonomous AI planning ability, potentially including sophisticated logistics and risk-assessment support for outdoor programs. But leading a camp activity for a special-needs population in an outdoor setting is a psychomotor, real-time, physically present task, and nothing in the observed capability trajectory targets outdoor supervisory leadership specifically; task-exposure research's physical/manual distinction is not expected to erode simply because planning tools improve. Diffusion evidence already shows firm-level AI adoption lagging capability by a wide margin, and small, specialized camp programs for special populations are a plausible late-adopter niche even under strong capability growth. The verification burden tied to outdoor, safety-critical supervision of a vulnerable population keeps a present human leader structurally necessary under any adoption scenario considered here. Given the sparse course description, this ten-year read should be treated as a directional estimate rather than a precise one.
HSL 1430.d: This class will provide information concerning methods and techniques applicable to camps for special populations and to outdoor recreational outings.

r: HSL 1500 delivers departmental skill requirements across variable physical-behavior topics for human performance, sport, and recreation majors and minors, combining teaching-methods instruction, field-experience assignments, and a cognitive component of readings, writing, and testing. This mixed structure maps to O*NET's Training and Teaching Others and Performing General Physical Activities alongside a smaller Documenting/Recording Information component. The lab and field-experience elements are embodied and require direct physical skill demonstration and supervision, which task-exposure research classifies as low-exposure manual work; the cognitive testing and reading component is more exposed but represents a minority share of the course. The binding constraint is the explicit departmental mandate — this course exists specifically to satisfy required physical-behavior skill competencies for the major — combined with the need for an instructor physically present to assess psychomotor skill performance, which is not achievable through AI-mediated assessment at this horizon.

By 2031, the reading, writing, and testing side of HSL 1500 could see meaningful AI involvement — generating study materials, grading written assignments, even tutoring — consistent with task-exposure research's finding that writing-adjacent tasks are strongly, positively associated with exposure. But the course's departmental purpose is explicitly to meet skill requirements in physical behaviors through field-experience assignments and laboratory activities, and that embodied component resists this trend; task-exposure research maintains the opposite classification for manual, physically demonstrated work. Verification burden is mixed — written testing can plausibly be AI-graded with light spot-checking, while psychomotor skill assessment in field placements still needs an instructor's direct judgment. Because the departmental mandate names physical-behavior skill competencies specifically, not merely general knowledge, the instrumental need to take this particular course for its lab and field components should persist even as its cognitive component becomes more AI-augmented on the margins.

At a ten-year horizon, METR/Epoch capability trends suggest the cognitive component of HSL 1500 — reading comprehension, written testing, even some tutoring — could be substantially AI-mediated, and task-exposure research's programming-and-writing-positive association gives some support to that expectation. The field-experience and laboratory skill-demonstration components are a different case: they require an instructor to physically observe and certify psychomotor competence in specific physical behaviors, a departmental requirement unlikely to be satisfied by simulated or remote assessment even as general AI capability grows, since the mandate is defined around embodied skill performance itself, not just knowledge of it. Diffusion research shows adoption trailing capability broadly, and departmental skill-requirement structures in applied physical-education programs are conservative, slow-changing institutional features. On balance, this course likely retains its instrumental role for its physical-skill and field components while its cognitive-assessment layer becomes increasingly AI-assisted, an outcome that should be read as directional given real uncertainty this far out.
HSL 1500.d: These courses are required for human performance and sports and recreation professions majors and minors to meet departmental skill requirements in various physical behaviors. They also cover methods of teaching and field experience assignments. All HSL 1500 courses include a cognitive component with written and reading assignments, testing, and assigned laboratory activities. Exercise Science
